title: Memoir
text:
*صفدر ماما جي*
کلا کلا راتا ډېر زيات ته را ياد شې ماما جي
ځکه مې په خولے جړه فر ياد شي ماما جي
نور څوک نشته دی چې ستا کمې پوره کړي
خالي خالي بہ اوس حاجي اباد شي ماما جي
ستا ځواني او بزرګي بلکه ټول عمر مثالي وو
بل به څوک زما رهبر زما استاد شي ماما جي
د ټول کلي رونق وې، ښکلا د هر محفل وې
پېشہ دې د ډاکټر وه، د پوهې نه وکيل وې
غٹ دروېش وې، هم ولي او هم کفيل وې
د هر زخم مرهم وې، د خوږو اوبو سبيل وې
ناڅاپه پر ےوزم په سجده شم په جړه شم
ستامحبت او احسانونه چې را ياد شي ماما جي
بيا دعا ته لاس اوچت کړمه الله ته پہ زاری شم
اوچته مرتبہ او جنتونه  د جائيداد شي ماما جي

title: Mamajee: A Life of Faith, Compassion and Enduring Legacy
text:
In Loving Memory of Col. Muhammad Safdar Khan (Mamajee)

Colonel Muhammad Safdar Khan, lovingly known to all as Mamajee, passed away peacefully on 17 July 2026 at CMH Rawalpindi. In his final moments, he was surrounded by those who cherished him most—his close family, dear relatives, and lifelong friends—an enduring testament to a life deeply rooted in love, compassion, and human connection.

Born and raised in a small village in the Charsadda district, Mamajee carried the simplicity and warmth of his origins throughout his life. He belonged to a large, closely-knit extended family and remained at its heart, particularly beloved by the younger generation. His gentle demeanor, approachable nature, and ever-smiling presence made him stand apart. Unlike many elders of our family who were known for their sternness and rigid discipline, Mamajee was the embodiment of kindness and ease. He was not only the favorite among the youth of our family but also admired and respected by the entire area.

Two qualities define the essence of his character: forgiveness and generosity. He was a man who never believed in revenge; no matter the circumstance, he chose to forgive. His heart carried no bitterness. Equally remarkable was his respect for others and his instinctive generosity—especially in helping those in financial need. These were not occasional virtues but habits of being. He seemed to distribute forgiveness and financial help as though they were his personal gifts to the world, quietly transforming lives along the way.

Such was his warmth and fatherly affection that everyone—family members, acquaintances, and even household staff—called him Mamajee. It was not merely a nickname; it was a reflection of the comfort and belonging he offered to all who crossed his path.

On a deeply personal note, I owe him more than words can express. As his nephew, and having lost my father even before I was born, I found in him a constant source of care and support. He never let me feel alone and, in many ways, treated me with a closeness that surpassed all others. His presence in my life was not just that of an elder—it was that of a guardian, a mentor, and a father figure.

He had an extraordinary sense of responsibility toward others, especially when it came to matters of health and well-being. Living in Rawalpindi, he became a trusted point of contact for people from surrounding villages who sought medical assistance. It was common for individuals—even those who barely knew him—to visit his home and stay overnight. I recall one particular instance when a group of strangers from Charsadda arrived unexpectedly seeking shelter. Concerned, I advised him to be cautious. He simply smiled and said, “Allah Malik hai—what can I do? They need a place for the night.” That was who he was: a man whose faith and humanity overrode all hesitation.

His generosity was boundless and often went beyond what was asked of him. Once, a friend requested him to lend a modest sum to his daughter for her children’s school fees. When she visited Mamajee and shared her broader financial struggles, he quietly handed her an envelope. Upon reaching home and opening it, she was astonished to find a much larger amount than expected. When her father later questioned Mamajee, he calmly replied, “Brother, that is a gift from my side. There is nothing to return.”

I never once saw him count money, regardless of the amount. He would often say, “If Allah grants me without counting, why should I count?” This rare and beautiful quality—complete detachment from material measure—was not only a hallmark of his character but also a legacy reflected in his children even after his passing.

He was a man of remarkable intellect and cultural depth. A gifted linguist, he spoke Persian, Arabic, Hebrew, Bengali, and Punjabi with ease besides other languages spoken in Pakistan, and could recite poetry in each of these languages. His love for literature and language added another dimension to his already rich personality.

His home was a place of constant hospitality, always open and welcoming. It was not unusual to find an extraordinary mix of guests under his roof—ambassadors, ministers, religious scholars, tribal elders, political figures, old colleagues from King Edward Medical College, friends from Europe, and villagers from his hometown. Yet, regardless of status or background, he treated everyone with the same respect, warmth, and sincerity. In his presence, distinctions dissolved; only humanity remained.

His trusting nature was both his strength and, at times, his vulnerability. I remember when he once considered purchasing a residential plot. I referred a property dealer to him, who later told me that Mamajee simply pointed to the most expensive plot on the map and said, “Please buy it. I trust you—I don’t have time to visit.” Such was the ease with which he placed his faith in others. While some unfortunately took advantage of this and caused him financial loss, he never expressed regret or bitterness. His response remained constant: “Allah Malik hai. Allah is the greatest.”

Despite these experiences, the overwhelming majority of his friends were sincere and deeply devoted to him. During his final days in the ICU, I would visit him at odd hours to ensure he was not alone. Time and again, I witnessed his friends standing beside him, tears in their eyes, speaking of him with profound love and admiration. It was then that I truly understood the depth of the lives he had touched.

One evening during discussion, I gently asked him if he had any regrets in life. After a brief pause, he said, “Yes, I wish I had spent more time with my parents during their last years.” I tried to reassure him, reminding him that he had done his best to be there whenever his duties allowed. But he looked at me with quiet conviction and replied, “Mumtaz, jobs don’t matter—they are temporary. What truly matters is love and prayers.”

He was also a proud veteran who served with distinction in three major conflicts—the wars of 1965 and 1971, and the 1973 Arab-Israel war. His service to the nation was marked by courage and dedication, yet he wore his achievements with humility.

Beyond his military career, he was a committed philanthropist. He quietly supported numerous welfare initiatives and helped educate individuals who otherwise could not have afforded it. His contributions were often made without recognition, driven solely by a genuine desire to uplift others.

An avid traveler, he journeyed extensively across Europe, the Middle East, the United States, Australia, and many other parts of the world. These travels gave him not only a broad perspective on different cultures and civilizations but also a rare first-hand understanding of the world's religions and traditions.

His extensive study of the Holy Qur'an, Hadith, Islamic history, and comparative religion, combined with close friendships with eminent religious scholars, transformed him into a living encyclopedia of religions, particularly Islam. His knowledge was not merely academic; it was balanced with wisdom, intellectual honesty, and an unwavering commitment to truth.

He firmly rejected sectarianism, ethnic prejudice, and racism, believing that these divisions weakened both society and the true spirit of faith. On several occasions, I witnessed him engage with sectarian scholars in calm and respectful debate. Drawing upon logic, historical evidence, and authoritative references from the scholars' own traditions, he would present his arguments with such clarity and depth that even the most ardent opponents found themselves without a convincing reply.

Those who knew him will remember not only the breadth of his knowledge but also his humility, fairness, and deep respect for human dignity. His life stands as a testament to the power of learning, open-mindedness, and principled conviction. He will be remembered with admiration and gratitude by all who had the privilege of knowing him.

He leaves behind a loving family—his devoted wife, two sons, and three daughters—who will undoubtedly carry forward his legacy of kindness, generosity, and service. Through them, and through the countless lives he touched, his spirit will continue to inspire.

He was not just a man of kind nature; he was an institution of compassion, a beacon of generosity, and a rare soul who lived with unwavering faith and selflessness.
His life reminds us that true greatness lies not in what we accumulate, but in what we give.

His funeral was held on the afternoon of 18 July 2026 in his native village of Haji Abad, Charsadda, where a vast gathering of relatives, friends, colleagues, admirers, and people from every walk of life came together to bid him a final farewell. Their presence bore witness to the respect, affection, and lasting impact he had on all who knew him.
His Janaza prayer was led by the revered Peer Sahib of Gorla Sharif, with whom he shared a lifelong bond of mutual love, respect, and spiritual devotion. It was a deeply moving farewell, reflecting not only the esteem in which he was held but also the values of faith, humility, and compassion that defined his life.
Colonel Muhammad Safdar Khan was laid to eternal rest in his ancestral graveyard in Charsadda, beside his beloved granddaughter, Sahar, and close to his cherished parents. There was a quiet poignancy in this final resting place—a reunion with those he loved most.
His burial serves as a gentle reminder of the profound truth of human existence: regardless of our achievements, status, or the journeys we undertake, we all return to the very earth upon which we once walked. In the end, it is not wealth or position that endures, but the love we shared, the lives we touched, and the legacy of kindness, honour, and integrity we leave behind.
Though Colonel Muhammad Safdar Khan is no longer among us, his memory will continue to live in the hearts of his family, friends, and all those whose lives were enriched by his presence. He will be remembered with deep love, immense pride, and enduring gratitude. May Allah grant him the highest place in Jannat-ul-Firdous and envelop him in His infinite mercy. Ameen.

With heartfelt prayers for his eternal peace,

Mumtaz Ali Khan

title: کرنل ڈاکٹر محمد صفدر خان کے ساتھ گزارے چھبیس سال کا خلاصہ
text: کرنل محمد صفدر خان کے ساتھ مجھے تقریباً چھبیس سال کام کرنے کا شرف حاصل ہوا۔ اس طویل عرصے میں میں نے انہیں ہمیشہ نہایت نیک، بااخلاق، دیانتدار اور باوقار انسان پایا۔ ان کا نرم لہجہ، اعلیٰ کردار اور دوسروں کے ساتھ حسنِ سلوک ہر ایک کے دل میں ان کے لیے احترام پیدا کر دیتا تھا۔ خصوصاً غریب اور ضرورت مند لوگوں کے ساتھ ان کی شفقت، ہمدردی اور فیاضی قابلِ تقلید تھی۔ میری ذاتی رائے میں وہ ایسے نیک سیرت انسان تھے جنہیں دیکھ کر اللہ کے نیک بندوں کی یاد آتی تھی۔ انہوں نے اپنی زندگی اپنے کردار، اخلاق اور انسان دوستی سے بے شمار لوگوں کے دلوں میں زندہ کر دی۔ اللہ تعالیٰ ان پر اپنی بے شمار رحمتیں نازل فرمائے، ان کے درجات بلند کرے اور ان کی نیکیوں کو ان کے لیے صدقۂ جاریہ بنائے۔ آمین۔

title: The magic word "Bachay"
text:
The Magic Word "Bachay": How One Word Can Disarm Any Room
Every family or community has that one figure who can settle a heated argument with a quiet smile, or turn a hostile moment into a peaceful agreement. For us, that was Safdar Mama Ji.
Mama Ji possessed a natural charisma and a deeply helpful nature, but his real superpower lay in a single, carefully chosen magic word: "Bachay."
Translating literally to "my child" or "son," the word itself is common enough. But when spoken by Mama Ji, it carried a weight of genuine warmth, care, and paternal wisdom that was utterly disarming. It didn't matter if he was speaking to an angry doctor, a frustrated mechanic, a defiant student, or simply someone a few years younger than him—the moment "Bachay" left his lips, the atmosphere shifted. Even the most rebellious individuals would drop their defenses and yield to his guidance.
He didn't toss the word around casually, either. Mama Ji used it sparingly, reserving it for moments when a conversation needed heart rather than heat. Because it was never forced, it never felt like a trick; it was a pure expression of human warmth.

title: Col Safdar is my uncle.
text:
Beyond the Name: How “Col Safdar Is My Uncle” Built an Officer
**By Habibullah**
Every family has a phrase that echoes through generations, but in mine, five words defined my entire youth: *“Col Safdar is my uncle.”*
For years, that simple sentence was my armor, my key to open doors, and my ultimate source of confidence. It was 1992, and I was a 7th-grade student sitting across from Col Jan Gul Khattak, the formidable Principal of Cadet College Razmak. I had passed the written entry exam and was now facing the final hurdle: the interview.
When the Principal asked about my father’s profession, I proudly offered a two-part answer: *"He is a farmer, but Col Safdar is my uncle."*
The Principal smiled, perhaps amused by my absolute conviction, and repeated the question. I held my ground and gave the exact same reply. Whether out of merit or the charm of a young boy's fierce loyalty to his uncle's name, I was admitted.
Throughout six rigorous years at Razmak, followed by the high-stakes evaluation at the ISSB and medical checks at CMH, that phrase acted like a life-saving drug. My uncle’s reputation was a towering canopy under which I walked safely.
### The Challenge
The true turning point came on the eve of my departure for Karachi to join the Pakistan Naval Academy. Before I stepped onto the path to becoming a naval officer, Col Safdar pulled me aside.
> *"My name has been a source of recognition for you,"* he said quietly. *"But do you know what would make me even prouder?"*
> *"What, Mama Ji?"* I asked.
> *"I want your name to be a source of recognition for me."*
>
I stood silent. The weight of his expectation hung in the air—not as a burden, but as a challenge to build an identity of my own.
I left for Karachi, endured two intense years of military and naval training, and earned my commission as a Sub-Lieutenant. Shortly after, I was posted to the Pakistan Navy Engineering College (PNEC) to pursue my Bachelor’s Degree in Electronics Engineering. Even as commissioned officers, our trainee routine remained strict. Movement in and out of the base, visiting hours, and guest allowances were tightly regulated.
### A Surprise Visit at the Gate
One afternoon, a message came from the main security gate: *Guests are waiting for you.*
Unaware of any planned visit, I hurried down, slightly anxious. Standing in the waiting room was Col Safdar himself. He was in Karachi to visit his daughter, Zainab, and had decided to drop by my college across the road. Knowing how little my uncle tolerated delays and red tape, I immediately braced myself to apologize for keeping him waiting.
Before I could open my mouth, he looked at me and spoke words I will never forget:
*"Finally, you have made me proud."*
Confused, I began, *"Mama Ji, I am so sorry for these stupid procedures they have at the gate—"*
He cut me off with a smile. *"No, really. You have made me proud today, and you have become my source of recognition."*
He went on to explain what had happened at the guard post. When the duty personnel asked for his identity, he replied as he always had: *"I am Col Safdar."*
The guard looked up and said, *"Okay, you are Col Safdar, but what is the purpose of your visit?"*
My uncle had to answer: *"Sub-Lieutenant Habibullah is my nephew."*
Only then did the gates open for him—not as a Colonel, but as the guest of S-Lt Habibullah.
### "He Is With Me"
That day, the roles reversed completely. I took my uncle on a tour across various Naval units in Karachi. I sat in the front passenger seat next to the driver, while Col Safdar sat in the rear.
At every security checkpoint, the routine played out in sweet reversal. I would lean out, present my official service card, and receive a salute from the guards. Then came the inevitable question: *"Sir, who is the gentleman in the back seat?"*
I would look back, meet my uncle's eye in the rearview mirror, and tell the guard: **"He is with me."**
I said it at every gate, letting the words carry all the gratitude and pride I had carried since class 7.
After touring several establishments, my uncle finally laughed and threw his hands up. *"Alright, enough of this pride thing! Now take me somewhere nice that isn't a naval base."*
I followed his orders immediately.
Looking back, those five words—*"Col Safdar is my uncle"*—didn't just give me an identity when I was young; they gave me a standard to live up to. And standing at the gate of PNEC, watching my mentor beam with pride, I realized the greatest honor of my life wasn't just bearing his legacy, but earning the right to share it.

In Loving Memory of Colonel Sahib

Remembering our dear Colonel Sahib brings a deep sense of affection, gratitude and sadness. He was a truly special person, exceptional in his love for his friends, his family, his people, its history, and dedication to his work and his country, yet equally remarkable in his intellect, understanding, generosity and acceptance of people and perspectives different from his own.

What touched me most was his truly exceptional intellect and his down to earth loving persona that carried the warmth and continuity of his lifelong association that he adoringly preserved and carried, even with the children of his friends and associates long after they had left. Colonel Sahib continued to remember them with such kindness and affection. He kept those memories alive, and in doing so kept a precious connection with our family alive too.

He was always there to help, to support and to encourage quietly, generously and without expectation. There was something deeply reassuring about him: his wisdom, his humanity and his extraordinary capacity to understand.

Colonel Sahib was one of those rare people whose presence enriched the lives of those around him. I feel privileged to have listened to some of his accounts of his very rich life and am deeply grateful that I did get that rare opportunity.

He was truly one of a kind. May Allah bless his soul and grant him the highest place in Jannat-ul-Firdous. May his memory always remain a blessing.

title: In Memory of of a Noble soul
text:
In Memory of a Noble Soul

The loss of a truly honourable person is felt far beyond the family.
My great uncle will always be remembered as a man of wisdom, humility, and unwavering dedication.
His life reflected excellence, integrity, and a deep commitment to serving others.

Although I had only two brief conversations on phone with him while I was at the hospital with his brother, Professor Muhammad Israr, his kindness and humility left a lasting impression on me.
His passing is a great loss to our family and to everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.
May Allah (SWT) forgive his shortcomings, grant him the highest place in Jannah, and bless his family with patience and strength.
Ameen.

title: The Heart of our family
text:
*Some lives cannot be measured in years. They are measured in the lives they uplift, the values they instill, and the love they leave behind.* Our beloved grandfather, *Col (R) Dr. Muhammad Safdar Khan*, lived such a life.

He was a man of honor, compassion, wisdom, and unwavering integrity.In the clinic, he healed with knowledge and kindness. And at home, he led with a quiet strength that made him the true pillar of our family.

More than his achievements and titles, it was his character that defined him. He taught us through his actions that greatness is not about recognition. It is about humility when you have the power to be proud. It is about choosing honesty when it is difficult. It is about giving your time, your care, and your wisdom to others without expecting anything in return.

He believed in learning, in service, and in doing the right thing even when no one was watching. His stories made us wiser. His advice made us stronger. His love made us feel safe.

Though he has returned to Allah, his presence remains with us. His values guide our decisions. His lessons shape how we treat people. And his memories keep him alive in our hearts and in the hearts of the generations to come.

*May Allah (SWT) forgive his shortcomings, expand his grave with light and peace, and grant him the highest rank in Jannat-ul-Firdous. Ameen.*

The memory is of importance to me because of my Father, who were not only related to Colonel Sahib due to his profession but also because of belonging to same town.

My father had depression problem and used to take treatment from CMH but before going to any other Doc, Colonel sahib used to be his point of contact and then Colonel sahib used to accompany him and take him to the Dr himself on all visits.

Even I recall that Lala, sent other patients to CMH and his good self, and my father's small chit would be highly regarded.

Last but not the least, he is also father in law of my closed friend Arif Khan and also Ali Gohar Lala, May Allah bless him high Muqaam in Jannah

title: Words I Will Never Forget
text:
In 2016, my mother was scheduled to undergo open heart surgery at AFIC. All four of her arteries were blocked, and I was overwhelmed with stress and anxiety.

Before the surgery, I went to see Safdar Kaka at Hearts International Hospital, where he was serving at the time. As soon as he saw me, he asked, "Why are you so stressed?" I shared my fears about my mother's condition.

He called a doctor from the operating theatre and asked him to take me inside. Puzzled, I replied, "Why would I go to the OT? I am not a doctor."

He smiled and said, "Watch three surgeries, and you will be able to perform the fourth." Then, with his usual calm confidence, he added, "Son, it is such an easy surgery that even you can perform."

Those few words completely changed my perspective. My fear gave way to trust and confidence. That was Safdar Kaka's remarkable gift. He had an extraordinary ability to reassure people and fill them with courage, even in their most difficult moments.

May Allah grant him the highest place in Jannah. Ameen.

A Tribute to the Life and Legacy of Col. Muhammad Safdar Khan (Late) “A legend “

There are individuals whose lives transcend the ordinary and whose presence becomes an institution in itself. Their passing is not merely the loss of a beloved family member but the end of an era. Col. Muhammad Safdar Khan was one such extraordinary soul whose departure has left a profound void that will be exceedingly difficult to fill. Society seldom witnesses personalities of such remarkable stature, integrity, wisdom, and selfless devotion.

He was far more than a highly respected Army officer and an accomplished cardiac pathologist. He was a devoted father, a compassionate mentor, an exemplary Pakhtoon elder, a distinguished scholar, a gifted poet, a humble Sufi, a visionary social reformer, a champion of interfaith harmony, a trusted advisor to political leaders, and a tireless advocate of justice and humanity. A Ghazi of three wars—the 1965 Indo-Pak War, the 1971 War, and the Arab-Israel War—he served his country and the Muslim Ummah with extraordinary courage, unwavering honour, and unshakeable commitment. His bravery in uniform was matched only by his humility, grace, and kindness in civilian life.

Throughout his life, Col. Safdar Khan stood firmly for the dignity and empowerment of women, believing that no society can truly prosper without recognizing their rightful place and contribution. He championed social justice, dedicated himself to charitable and humanitarian causes, and devoted countless hours to the welfare of the less fortunate. He was equally cherished by children, admired by elders, respected by colleagues, and deeply loved by friends. His wisdom brought comfort, his counsel inspired confidence, his generosity restored hope, and his character earned the admiration of all who had the privilege of knowing him.

His legacy cannot be measured by the distinguished positions he held or the honours he received, but by the countless lives he touched, the values he upheld, and the enduring inspiration he leaves behind. He built bridges where others saw divisions, spread compassion where there was despair, and instilled courage where there was uncertainty. His life remains a timeless example of honour, humility, intellectual brilliance, faith, and service to humanity.

The vacuum created by the passing of such a towering personality cannot easily be filled. Yet, while his physical presence is no longer with us, his noble ideals, unwavering principles, and enduring legacy will continue to illuminate the path for generations to come. His memory will forever remain a source of inspiration for his family, friends, students, admirers, and all whose lives were enriched by his extraordinary character.

May Almighty Allah envelop Col. Muhammad Safdar Khan in His boundless mercy, forgive all his shortcomings, elevate his rank among the righteous, and grant him the highest place in Jannat-ul-Firdous. May his grave be filled with Divine light, peace, and everlasting tranquillity. May Allah bless his beloved family, siblings, relatives, friends, followers, and all who mourn his loss with patience, strength, unity, and steadfast faith. May He enable us all to honour his memory by carrying forward the values of courage, compassion, wisdom, justice, and service that defined his remarkable life. Ameen.

--------------------------
ڈاکٹر محمد صفدر خان کا سفر آخرت
------------------------------------
18جولائی  2026ء

بچھڑا کچھ  اس ادا سے کہ رت ہی بدل گئی
اک شخص سارے شہر کو ویران کر کیا

یہ شعر کئی دفعہ پڑھا ۔ کئی دفعہ سنا مگر کبھی اس کی تجسیم نہیں دیکھی تھی، کبھی اس کی چبھن محسوس نہیں کی، کبھی یہ سوچا نہیں تھا کہ یہ تو دل کا بیانیہ ہے جب اس کی ناؤ ڈوبتی ہے۔
محمد صفدر خان خالق حقیقی سے جا ملے ۔  بے شک   ایک دن اس کو جانا تھا ۔  فنا سے کسی پیغمبر کو استثناء نہیں ۔ وہ تو ہماری طرح مٹی کی مورت تھے ۔ اس کو ابدیت کی سند کون دیتا ؟ ہمیشہ رہنے والی ذات تو صرف اللہ کی ہے ۔
یہ  سب کچھ درست ، مگر دل تو دیوانہ ہوتا ہے۔ اس پر کس کا قابو ہے۔ سوچتا ہوں، کاش وہ ابھی نہ جاتے ۔۔۔۔۔
صفدر خان کی زندگی کو اگر ایک لفظ میں بیان کرنے کی شرط رکھی جائے تو بلا تردد میرا جواب ہو گا،  " محبت"۔ وہ سراپا محبت تھے۔ اس سفر میں  وہ ان رفعتوں کو پا چکے تھے جہاں محبوب کی ہر ادا انسان کو وجد میں لاتی ہے ۔ جہاں ہجر اپنے معنی کھو بیٹھتا ہے اور وصال کے خم ہر لمحہ لنڈھائے جاتے ہیں۔ میں نے اپنی پہلی کتاب " آشفتہ بیانی" میں ان کے تین واقعات کا ذکر کیا ہے۔ اپنی بیٹیوں سے محبت کا واقعہ قارئین کے لیے  پیش خدمت ہے۔
-------------------------------------
یہ جگر گوشے

صفدر خان کی شہرت ایک اچھے ڈاکٹر کی تھی۔ دوستوں میں ہردلعزیز تھے۔ مگر ان کی جس خوبی نے مجھے ان کا گرویدہ بنایا وہ اپنی بیٹیوں کے ساتھ ان کا حسنِ سلوک تھا۔
عائشہ، زینب۔ اور سعدیہ  ۔۔۔۔ خوبصورت نام رکھے تھے۔ سب سے بڑی بیٹی بمشکل نو سال کی ہو گی۔ بنوں چھاؤنی میں واقع اپنے گھر کے وسیع لان میں شام کو وہ سائیکل پر آپس میں ریسں لگاتیں تو ڈاکٹر صاحب ریفری بن جاتے۔ اس ریس میں کوئی بھی دوسری پوزیشن حاصل نہیں کرتا تھا۔ ڈاکٹر صاحب اعلان کر دیتے کہ نو سال کی Category میں عائشہ نے اوّل پوزیشن حاصل کی ہے۔ بچّوں کی کیٹیگری میں سعدیہ نے میدان مار لیا ہے۔
سائیکل ریس کا مرحلہ ختم ہو جاتا تو بچیاں مٹھی میں بڑے بڑے اخروٹ داب لیتیں اور پوچھتیں کس ہاتھ میں چھپایا ہے؟ اخروٹ اتنے بڑے ہوتے کہ باہر سے نظر آ جاتے تھے۔ مگر ڈاکٹر صاحب دوسرے ہاتھ کی طرف اشارہ کر دیتے۔۔۔۔۔
وہ خوشی سے اچھل پڑتیں۔ ’’ابّو سے ہم نے مقابلہ جیت لیا ہے۔‘‘
نوکر چائے لے آتا تو ڈاکٹر صاحب پوچھ لیتے۔ ’’آج کس کی باری ہے چائے بنانے کی۔‘‘
مجھے یاد نہیں پڑتا کہ عائشہ اور اس کی بہنوں میں کبھی ’باری‘ پر اتفاق ہوا ہو۔ آپس میں لڑ پڑتیں۔ ڈاکٹر صاحب بیچ بچاؤ کروا  دیتے۔
’’اچھا! ایک انکل کے لئے بنائیں اور میں دو کپ پی لوں گا۔ اب خوش۔‘‘
عائشہ کی ماں روز کہتیں ’’سر پر چڑھا رکھا ہے ان کو، پرائے گھر جائیں گی پھر ان کے نخرے کون اٹھائے گا۔‘‘
ڈاکٹر صاحب کا رویہ بدلا نہ ان کی بیگم کے تبصرے۔ دیکھتے دیکھتے سال گزر گیا۔ صفدر خان کی ترقی ہوئی، راولپنڈی چلے گئے۔ میں بھی سی ۔ایس ۔ایس کا امتحان پاس کرکے ٹریننگ کے لئے عازمِ لاہور ہوا۔
O
تینوں بیٹیاں اب پیا کے گھر سدھار گئی ہیں۔ اپنے والدین کے گھر آتی جاتی ہیں۔ البتہ اب ڈاکٹر صاحب کے قریب کی کرسیاں ان کے نواسے، نواسیوں نے سنبھال لی ہیں۔
O
حدیث شریف: نبی مہربانﷺ نے ارشاد فرمایا: ’’جس کی تین بیٹیاں ہوں، وہ اُن کے ساتھ اچھا سلوک کرے تو اُس کے لئے جنّت واجب ہو جاتی ہے، عرض کیا: اور دو ہوں تو؟ فرمایا: دو ہوں تب بھی، عرض کیا: اگر ایک ہو تو؟ فرمایا: اگر ایک ہو تو بھی۔‘‘(معجم الاوسط، ج:4، ص: 347، حدیث 6199، ملحضاً)
attr: — Habibullah Khan Khattak, Family / Friend · 1977 · Bannu

title: Miss you mama ji
text:
Kala kala mey der zyaat ta rapa yaad shay mama ji
Zaka zaka mey pa khola jara faryaad shi mama ji
Noar soak nashta day che sta kamay pora kri
Sta na pas ba os khaali Haji Abad shi mama ji
Sta zwaani ao bazurgi balke toal omer be misal wu
Os ba cha na kawu zdakra os ba soak zamung ustaad shi mama ji
Da toal kali rawnaq way,khkula da har mehfil way
Paisha dey da Doctor wa, da pohay na wakeel way
Da zra na yaw darwaish way, hum wali ao hum kafeel way
Da har zakham marham way, da khwago obu sabeel way
Duaganay darpasey di che jannatuna Dey jaidaad shi mama ji
Za hum prewzam pa sajda, sta ihsanuna che rayaad shi mama ji
کله کله مې ډېر زیات ته راپاد شې ماما جي
ځکه ځکه مې په خوله ژړا فریاد شي ماما جي
نور څوک نشته دی چې ستا کمی پوره کړي
ستا نه پس به اوس خالي حاجي اباد شي ماما جي
ستا ځواني او بزرګي بلکې ټول عمر بې مثال وو
اوس به چا نه کوو زده کړه، اوس به څوک زموږ استاد شي ماما جي
د ټول کلي رونق وې، ښکلا د هر محفل وې
پېشه دې د ډاکټر وه، د پوهې نه وکیل وې
د زړه نه یو دروېش وې، هم ولي او هم کفیل وې
د هر  زخم مرهم وې، د خوږو اوبو سبیل وې
دعاوې درپسې دي چې جېنتونه دې جایداد شي ماما جي
زه هم پرېوځم په سجده، ستا احسانونه چې را یاد شي ماما جي

title: My Uncle
text:
ہمارے ماموں
کرنل ڈاکٹر محمد صفدر خان مہمندؒ
تحریر: ریاض خان
اگر اس تحریر کا عنوان "میرے ماموں" رکھا جائے تو شاید یہ ان کے ساتھ انصاف نہ ہو، کیونکہ وہ صرف میرے ماموں نہیں تھے، بلکہ یوں کہنا زیادہ مناسب ہوگا کہ وہ سب کے ماموں تھے۔
سگے بھانجوں کی بات کی جائے تو اللہ تعالیٰ نے انہیں دو بھائی اور چھ بہنیں عطا فرمائی تھیں، اور ہر بہن کی اولاد بھی، ماشاء اللہ، کسی چھوٹے خاندان سے کم نہ تھی۔ یوں سگے بھانجوں اور بھانجیوں کی تعداد ہی ایک لشکر معلوم ہوتی تھی۔ ان سب کے نام یاد رکھنا شاید سی ایس ایس کا امتحان پاس کرنے سے کم مشکل نہ ہوتا۔
لیکن حقیقت یہ ہے کہ ان کے بھانجے صرف وہی نہ تھے جن کا رشتہ خون سے تھا۔ ان کے بے شمار ایسے بھانجے بھی تھے جو محبت کے رشتے سے ان سے وابستہ تھے۔ کچھ منہ بولے، کچھ خود ساختہ، اور کچھ وہ جنہوں نے خود ہی اپنے آپ کو ان کا بھانجا قرار دے رکھا تھا۔ دلچسپ بات یہ تھی کہ ماموں کو اس سب کا علم بھی تھا، مگر انہوں نے کبھی کسی کی تردید نہیں کی۔ جو شخص بھی کہہ دیتا، "میں کرنل صاحب کا بھانجا ہوں"، وہ مسکرا کر فرماتے، "ہاں بھئی، یہ میرا بھانجا ہے۔"
مجھے اس سلسلے کا ایک واقعہ ہمیشہ یاد رہے گا۔
ایک مرتبہ میں ہارٹس انٹرنیشنل ہسپتال کی لیبارٹری میں ماموں کے دفتر گیا۔ وہاں ایک نوجوان پہلے سے بیٹھا ہوا تھا۔ میں اسے اچھی طرح جانتا تھا۔ وہ ایک نہایت غریب گھرانے سے تعلق رکھتا تھا اور ماموں خاموشی سے اس کی تعلیم اور گھر کے اخراجات برداشت کر رہے تھے۔
میں نے دیکھا کہ وہ اس اعتماد سے بیٹھا ہے کہ شاید میں نے ماموں کے اپنے بیٹوں کو بھی کبھی اس انداز میں بیٹھے نہ دیکھا ہو۔
میں نے پوچھا، "بھائی صاحب، آپ کا تعارف؟"
اس نے فوراً جواب دیا، "میں کرنل صاحب کا بھانجا ہوں۔"
پھر اس نے مجھ سے پوچھ لیا، "اور آپ کون ہیں؟"
میں نے عرض کیا، "جی، میں تو ان کا نوکر ہوں، لیبارٹری سے سیمپل لینے آیا ہوں۔"
اس وقت میرے پاس اس جواب کے علاوہ اور کوئی راستہ بھی نہ تھا۔ بھانجے کی نشست تو پہلے ہی کسی اور نے سنبھال رکھی تھی۔
ایک اور واقعہ بھی اسی نوعیت کا ہے۔
ایک جاننے والا مجھے ایک اعلیٰ سرکاری افسر سے ملوانے لے گیا۔ مجھے معلوم نہ تھا کہ وہ پہلے ہی اپنا تعارف کرنل صاحب کے بھانجے کی حیثیت سے کرا چکا ہے۔
گفتگو کے دوران اس افسر نے مجھ سے پوچھا، "یہ تو کرنل صاحب کے بھانجے ہیں، آپ ان کے کیا لگتے ہیں؟"
میں نے عرض کیا، "جی، وہ میرے پھوپھا ہیں۔"
اصل حقیقت یہ تھی کہ کرنل ڈاکٹر محمد صفدر خان مہمندؒ بیک وقت میرے سگے ماموں بھی تھے اور میری پھوپھی کے شوہر بھی۔ میں نے دل ہی دل میں سوچا کہ چلو، بھانجے والا رشتہ تو یہاں بھی کسی اور کے حصے میں گیا، کم از کم پھوپھا والا رشتہ ابھی محفوظ ہے۔
یہ واقعات بظاہر مزاحیہ ہیں، مگر ان کے پیچھے ایک بڑی حقیقت پوشیدہ ہے۔ ماموں کا دل اس قدر کشادہ تھا کہ ہر شخص خود کو ان کا اپنا سمجھتا تھا، اور وہ بھی کسی کو یہ احساس نہیں ہونے دیتے تھے کہ وہ ان سے دور ہے۔
ہمارا ان سے تعلق بھی عجیب تھا۔ ہم ان سے محبت بھی کرتے تھے، ان کا بے حد احترام بھی کرتے تھے، اور نہ جانے کیوں ان سے ڈرتے بھی تھے۔
یہ ڈر اس لیے نہیں تھا کہ انہوں نے کبھی کسی کو ڈانٹا یا سزا دی ہو، بلکہ اس لیے تھا کہ وہ خود بہت منظم اور اصول پسند انسان تھے، جبکہ ہم غلطیوں کے چلتے پھرتے نمونے تھے۔ عجیب اتفاق یہ تھا کہ میری اکثر غلطیاں بھی انہی کے سامنے ہوتیں، اس لیے جب بھی ان کے پاس جاتا، دل میں ایک ہلکا سا خوف ضرور ہوتا کہ آج نہ جانے کس بات پر میری پکڑ ہو جائے۔
مجھ پر انہوں نے بہت کوشش کی کہ میں سی ایس ایس کا امتحان دوں۔ ایک دن اپنے دفتر میں بیٹھے بیٹھے انہوں نے ایک پرچی پر لکھا:
"اگر ریاض نے سی ایس ایس کر لیا تو میں اپنا نام بدل دوں گا۔"
نیچے اپنے دستخط بھی کر دیے۔
میں نے ہنس کر عرض کیا، "ماموں، مجھے معلوم ہے آپ مجھے غیرت دلانے کی کوشش کر رہے ہیں، مگر آپ صرف اپنی توانائی ضائع کر رہے ہیں۔ اتنی لمبی غیرت مجھ سے نہیں نبھے گی۔"
وہ بھی مسکرا دیے، لیکن ان کی ہر کوشش کے پیچھے صرف ایک ہی جذبہ ہوتا تھا کہ ان کے اپنے لوگ زندگی میں آگے بڑھیں۔
ان کی شخصیت کا ایک اور حیرت انگیز پہلو ان کا علم تھا۔ میں نے زندگی میں شاید ہی کوئی ایسا شخص دیکھا ہو جس کی دلچسپی کا دائرہ اتنا وسیع ہو۔
میں نے میٹرک میں سائنس لی تو وہ فزکس، کیمسٹری، فلکیات اور کوانٹم فزکس پر گفتگو کرنے لگے۔ میں نے ایف اے میں ہیومینٹیز اختیار کی تو فلسفہ اور کارل مارکس زیرِ بحث آ گئے۔ گریجویشن میں انگریزی ادب لیا تو دل میں خوشی تھی کہ اب شاید کچھ بات بن جائے گی، مگر انہوں نے آغاز ہی کانٹ، ٹالسٹائی، نطشے اور قدیم فلسفیوں سے کیا۔ جب میں نے عرض کیا کہ "ماموں، یہ تو ہمارے نصاب میں نہیں تھا"، تو مسکرا کر فرمایا:
"بیٹا! لائبریری اسی لیے ہوتی ہے کہ آدمی نصاب سے آگے بھی پڑھے۔"
یہی ان کا انداز تھا۔ کسان آتا تو زراعت کی بات کرتے، ڈاکٹر آتا تو طب کی، انجینئر آتا تو انجینئرنگ کی، اور تاجر آتا تو تجارت کی۔ کمال یہ تھا کہ وہ کسی کو اپنی دنیا میں نہیں کھینچتے تھے، بلکہ خود اس کی دنیا میں جا کر اس سے گفتگو کرتے تھے۔
ہمارے خاندان میں انہیں کبھی کسی نے سردار منتخب نہیں کیا، نہ اس کی ضرورت پیش آئی۔ لوگ خود ان کی بات کو آخری بات سمجھتے تھے، کیونکہ ان میں ایک اچھے رہنما کی تمام صفات موجود تھیں۔ وہ صاحبِ علم تھے، صاحبِ کردار تھے، صاحبِ حیثیت تھے، مگر ان کی اصل طاقت خدمت تھی۔
کسی کا تھانے کا مسئلہ ہو، کسی کا مقدمہ ہو، زمین کا تنازع ہو، کسی نوجوان کو روزگار درکار ہو، کسی مریض کے علاج کی فکر ہو، یا کسی بچی کی شادی کا مرحلہ درپیش ہو، ماموں ہر جگہ سب سے آگے نظر آتے تھے۔
ایک مرتبہ انہوں نے مجھ سے کہا:
"ریاض! لوگ کہتے ہیں کہ دنیا میں چار چیزیں ہیں: حسن، دولت، قابلیت اور طاقت۔ مگر میں کہتا ہوں کہ پانچویں چیز خدمت ہے، اور یہی وہ نعمت ہے جسے کبھی زوال نہیں آتا۔"
آج ان کی زندگی پر نظر ڈالتا ہوں تو محسوس ہوتا ہے کہ اللہ تعالیٰ نے انہیں یہ پانچوں نعمتیں عطا فرمائی تھیں، مگر ان کی اصل پہچان خدمت تھی۔
ان کا دسترخوان ہمیشہ آباد رہتا تھا۔ میں نے شاید ہی کبھی ان کے گھر قدم رکھا ہو اور وہاں مہمان موجود نہ ہوں۔ جرنیل بھی ہوتے تھے، سیاست دان بھی، افسر بھی، اور انہی کے ساتھ کسی دور دراز گاؤں کا ایک غریب رشتہ دار بھی اسی عزت سے بیٹھا ہوتا تھا۔ ان کے نزدیک انسان کی قدر اس کے عہدے سے نہیں، اس کے کردار سے ہوتی تھی۔
شاید اسی لیے ہمارے خاندان میں ان کی سرداری کسی عہدے یا اختیار کی مرہونِ منت نہیں تھی۔ وہ دلوں کے سردار تھے، اور دلوں پر حکومت ووٹوں سے نہیں، کردار سے قائم ہوتی ہے۔
ایسے لوگ روز روز پیدا نہیں ہوتے۔ وہ ایک نسل کی تربیت کرتے ہیں اور پھر خاموشی سے رخصت ہو جاتے ہیں، مگر ان کی محبت، ان کی خدمت اور ان کی یاد ہمیشہ زندہ رہتی ہے۔

آج بھی کبھی خاندان کے کسی بزرگ کا
فون آتا ہے، یا کسی جرگے کی بات چھڑتی ہے، یا کسی بیمار، بے روزگار یا مجبور انسان کا ذکر ہوتا ہے تو بے اختیار دل کہتا ہے: "یہ کام تو ماموں کر دیتے۔" پھر یکایک یاد آتا ہے کہ اب فون ملانے کے لیے وہ نمبر موجود ہے، مگر دوسری طرف سے "ہاں ریاض، بتاؤ!" کہنے والی آواز ہمیشہ کے لیے خاموش ہو چکی ہے۔
ایسے لوگ مرتے نہیں، صرف نظروں سے اوجھل ہوتے ہیں۔ وہ اپنے کیے ہوئے احسانوں میں زندہ رہتے ہیں، اپنے سکھائے ہوئے سبقوں میں سانس لیتے ہیں، اور ان دلوں میں ہمیشہ آباد رہتے ہیں جنہیں انہوں نے کبھی ٹوٹنے نہیں دیا۔
اللہ تعالیٰ کرنل ڈاکٹر محمد صفدر خان مہمندؒ پر اپنی بے پایاں رحمتیں نازل فرمائے، ان کی لغزشوں سے درگزر فرمائے، ان کی قبر کو جنت کے باغوں میں سے ایک باغ بنا دے، اور ہمیں توفیق عطا فرمائے کہ ہم بھی ان کی طرح اپنے لیے نہیں، دوسروں کے لیے جینا سیکھیں۔ آمین۔

title: Remembering a Life Well Lived
text:
Our grandfather lived a life of purpose, dignity, and service. He was deeply respected for his achievements, but to us, he will always be remembered for his gentle nature, wise words, and the love he gave so freely to his family.

He was a source of strength in difficult times and a guiding presence in our lives. Through his actions, he taught us the importance of kindness, honesty, patience, and helping others without expecting anything in return.

His absence is deeply felt, yet the values he passed on and the memories he left behind will always remain in our hearts. We will continue to remember him with love, pride, and gratitude.

May Allah (SWT) shower him with mercy, forgive his shortcomings, make his grave peaceful and full of light, and grant him the highest ranks in Jannat al-Firdaws. Ameen.
attr: — QUAID IQBAL, Grandson · July 2026 · Education city, Doha, Qatar 🇶🇦

title: Humility as a fundamental principle
text:
There are people who leave behind wealth. Others leave behind titles, buildings, or accomplishments. And then there are the rare few who leave behind something far more valuable—they leave behind a way of living.

Dr. Muhammad Safdar Khan was one of those rare people.

If someone were to ask me what defined him, I would not begin by saying he was a doctor, although he healed thousands. I would not begin by saying he was a poet, although his words carried wisdom. I would not begin by saying he spoke many languages, although he could connect with people from every walk of life.

I would simply say this:

His religion was humanity.

He believed that every human being deserved dignity, compassion, and respect. He never asked where someone came from, what they believed, how much they owned, or what status they held. To him, every person was worthy of kindness simply because they were human.

He often lived by the timeless wisdom of the great Pashto poet, Rahman Baba:

ژوندے ځان په ځمکه ښخ کړه لکه تخم،
که لویئ غواړې، د خاورو په مقام شه.

“Bury yourself in the earth like a seed; if you seek greatness, embrace the humility of the soil.”

This was not merely poetry to him. It was his philosophy.

Like a seed, he believed that true greatness begins with humility. A seed does not become a mighty tree by standing proudly above the ground. It first allows itself to disappear into the darkness of the earth. It surrenders its pride, breaks open, and gives itself completely before new life can emerge.

That is how he lived.

He never sought recognition. He sought usefulness.

He never chased admiration. He earned respect.

He never measured success by what he accumulated, but by what he gave away.

As a physician, he healed bodies. As a poet, he nourished souls. As a father and grandfather, he built a family grounded in love, integrity, and service. His greatest lessons were rarely spoken; they were lived. Watching him was itself an education. In a world that often celebrates those who stand above others, he chose instead to stand beside them.

Perhaps that is why so many people loved him.

He taught us that humility is not weakness. It is strength under control. Service is not sacrifice. It is life’s highest privilege. Kindness is not softness. It is the purest expression of courage.

Looking back now, I realize that he was planting seeds everywhere he went. Every patient he comforted, every friend he encouraged, every child he guided, every stranger he helped became another seed of goodness.

Today, he has returned to the same earth that Rahman Baba wrote about.

Like the seed he admired, he now rests beneath the soil.

But seeds are never buried to disappear.

They are buried to grow.

His body has returned to the earth, but his character continues to grow in those who knew him. His kindness lives in the lives he touched. His wisdom lives in the words he left behind. His faith lives in the values he planted within his family.

That is the miracle of a life lived in humility.

The world loses a man.

But generations inherit his harvest.

May Allah accept every act of kindness he performed as an act of worship, forgive his shortcomings, illuminate his resting place, and grant him the everlasting gardens of Jannat al-Firdaws.

For those of us who remain, perhaps the greatest way to honour him is not merely to remember him.

It is to become another seed.
attr: — Ally Raza Qureshi, Son in law · Life long

title: Patience and Grace
text:
Lessons Left Behind by the Late Col (R) Dr. Safdar Khan
Great men leave behind many things—distinguished careers, commendable achievements, and honorable reputations. But the rarest and most enduring legacy a father can leave his children is the quiet, luminous wisdom forged through a life of faith, humility, and unconditional love.
The late Col (R) Dr. Safdar Khan was not merely a loving father; he was a gentle anchor for everyone around him. He possessed a profound understanding of human relationships, honoring every bond with grace and respect. In a world where personal grievances so easily fracture families, his approach to people was guided by a spiritual depth that continues to light the path for those he left behind.
A Lesson in Patience and Grace
One day, weighed down by the hurt and disappointment caused by the behavior of certain relatives, I went to him seeking comfort. Like any child reaching out to a parent, I expected empathy, perhaps even validation of my frustration.
Instead, he handed me a key to inner peace—a piece of timeless Urdu wisdom that he carried in his heart:
"اپنے آپ کو زمین کی طرح عاجز بناؤ اور ہوا کی طرح میسر کرو۔"
"Make yourself humble like the earth, and accessible like the wind—for everyone, especially your relatives."
Intrigued and moved by the poetical beauty of the advice, I asked him what it truly meant to be aajiz—humble—like the earth.
His response was breathtaking in its compassion:
"Look at the earth under our feet," he explained softly. "Everyone walks on it, presses against it, and steps over it. Yet, the earth never rebels. It never overthrows anyone from its surface in retaliation.
And when our journey in this world ends—when we reach our absolute weakest state in death—it is this very earth that wraps us in its gentle arms. It becomes our grave, offering us shelter, protection, and a dignity-saving cover (hijab) from a harsh world. The earth accepts us completely, with all our flaws, sins, and mistakes."
The Quiet Power of Humility
Through this profound metaphor, Col (R) Dr. Safdar Khan reframed how we ought to view human friction and strained relationships:
The Earth (Zameen): Teaches us ultimate resilience, patience, and silent forgiveness. It reminds us to endure life's small offenses with quiet strength and to offer protection and warmth to others, even when they may not deserve it.
The Wind (Hawa): Teaches us unconditional grace. The air does not choose whom it sustains; it offers life, breath, and comfort to all without distinction, ego, or expectation of return.
To live like the earth and the wind requires a heart free from pride. It means refusing to let bitterness harden our souls, choosing instead to respond to unkindness with vast, quiet generosity.
An Eternal Legacy
The late Col (R) Dr. Safdar Khan lived these words long before he spoke them. His life was a testament to the belief that true honor does not come from standing tall in pride, but from bending down in humility to lift others up.
Though he is no longer physically with us, his advice remains an eternal light. Every time life tests our patience or strains our bonds with loved ones, his words whisper softly across time, reminding us to be as patient as the earth beneath our feet, and as generous as the air we breathe.

title: A Life Guided by Faith and Service
text:
Some lives are measured not by years, but by the people they inspire. Our beloved grandfather was a man of honour, compassion, wisdom, and unwavering integrity.
More than a decorated officer and respected doctor, he was the pillar of our family. His humility, kindness, and dedication to serving others taught us that true greatness lies not in titles, but in living with sincerity and dignity.
Though he is no longer with us, his values, lessons, and loving memories will continue to guide generations.
May Allah (SWT) forgive his shortcomings, fill his grave with light and mercy, and grant him the highest place in Jannat al-Firdaws. Ameen.
